newsitem.title: FRANCE: Candidates snipe away as French election narrows.
newsitem.headline: Candidates snipe away as French election narrows.

text.p: French politicians intensified their campaign rhetoric on Friday as a new poll showed the opposition left gaining ground on the centre-right a little over a week before the first round of a parliamentary election.
Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin, in the southern city Toulouse, urged voters to punish the right by throwing it out of power just as they threw out the left in a 1993 election.

Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe, leading the government campaign, angrily tried to shoo his local Socialist opponent out of a marketplace in his Bordeaux constituency in south-west France when the two unexpectedly crossed paths in search of votes.

"If we disappointed the French people in 1993, and if they punished us, then they should take the same attitude today with the current majority. That's democracy," Jospin said in an interview on Sud Radio.

Jospin also turned the focus onto sleaze by branding Paris the "capital of opacity" in an attack targeting conservative President Jacques Chirac, who was mayor from 1977 to 1995, when he won the presidency.

"Corruption, scandals, networks of secret funding, cynical policies towards the poor and the young: Paris...has become the exclusive property of a few since 1997," he said in a late-night rally on Thursday.
Juppe dismissed charges that he was secretly preparing an amnesty to pardon political sleaze if his coalition wins the May 25-June 1 two-round election.
"It's pure fabrication," he told the daily Le Parisien. "There, as in other cases, justice will be done."
The opposition says the election was brought forward almost 10 months partly to stifle burgeoning cases of political corruption.
Juppe reacted angrily when he accidentally encountered Socialist candidate Gilles Savary while campaigning in the Dutertre marketplace, accompanied by a flock of reporters.
"Look at what you've been reduced to," Juppe snapped. "To get your picture taken, you have to stand near me."
"You're not around here very often, so I am taking advantage of that fact," snapped back Savary. "You're usually in Paris rather than Bordeaux."

A CSA poll for the French daily Parisien showed the race growing closer, predicting a centre-right margin of 43 seats over the combined left in the National Assembly, compared to a margin of 80 seats in a similar poll just three days earlier.
The pollsters, who questioned 1,008 registered voters on Thursday and Friday, concluded that the centre-right would win 299 assembly seats, the combined left 256, the far-right National Front none.
The earlier CSA survey had given the centre-right 317 seats to 237 seats for the left and one for the National Front.

As have other recent polls, the CSA survey indicated the combined left would win 40.5 percent of the first round vote to 38 percent for the centre-right, 7.5 percent for ecologist candidates and 14 percent for the National Front.
But it predicted the centre-right would emerge victorious in the June 1 run-off with support from National Front voters whose candidates did not survive the first-round.

In a sign the government could be reaching out to Front voters, Junior Minister for Urban Affairs Eric Raoult told Europe 1 radio that immigrants should wear a suit and tie to become a part of French society.

"Mamadou, if he is here legally, must wear a suit and tie, his wife must respect the laws of this country," Raoult said. Many of France's African immigrants wear the flowing robes typical of their home countries rather than a coat and tie,
